summary: Axis Bank keeps people’s and companies’ money in accounts and deposits and lends it out as home, car, gold, personal and business loans. It also issues cards, handles UPI phone payments (India’s instant bank transfers) and owns fund and broking firms.
description: A bank takes in money that people and businesses deposit, keeps it safe, lets them pay and withdraw it, and lends much of it to borrowers who pay interest. Axis does this through 6,278 branches in India, 12,796 cash machines and its phone app. It began in 1994 as UTI Bank and was renamed Axis Bank in 2008. In the year to March 2023 it bought Citibank’s consumer banking business in India. Around the bank sit companies it controls: Axis Finance lends, Axis Asset Management runs mutual funds, Axis Securities buys and sells shares for clients and Axis Capital advises companies raising money.
money: Most income is interest. Borrowers pay interest on loans, and the bank earns interest on government bonds it holds. From this it pays interest to depositors; what is left, net interest income, was about two-thirds of its operating revenue in 2025–26. Fees for cards, payments, selling investments and services to companies bring in most of the rest. It spends on staff, branches and technology, and sets money aside for loans that may not be repaid. A deposit is money the bank owes back, so it is not income, and income is not profit.
customers: Savers and borrowers are both customers. Individuals keep salaries and savings in accounts and fixed deposits, and the bank pays them interest. Home buyers, car buyers, people pledging gold, card users and small businesses borrow and pay interest; loans to individuals were 55% of all its loans in March 2026, with home loans the biggest part. Large and mid-sized companies borrow and pay fees for payments and trade services. Shops take card payments on its machines.
drivers: The gap between what it earns on loans and what it pays for deposits, how many borrowers repay on time, and whether it can gather enough deposits cheaply as its loans grow.

groups.title: Accounts and deposits
groups.examples: A salary savings account used through the bank’s ‘open’ mobile app, a shop’s current account or a fixed deposit.
groups.explanation: Places to keep money. Savings and current accounts pay little or no interest, so they are the bank’s cheapest money. A fixed deposit locks money away for a set time in return for a higher interest rate.

groups.title: Loans to individuals
groups.examples: A home loan, a car loan, a loan against gold jewellery, a personal loan or a credit card bill.
groups.explanation: The bank lends and collects interest and repayments. Home, car and gold loans are secured: the bank can sell the house, car or gold if the loan is not repaid. Personal loans and card spending are unsecured, so they charge more interest and lose more when borrowers stop paying.

groups.title: Cards and payments
groups.examples: Credit and debit cards, UPI payments from a phone and card machines in shops.
groups.explanation: Card users pay interest when they do not clear the bill in full, and the bank earns fees on card spending. Payments keep customers using the bank every day, which helps it hold their deposits.

groups.title: Loans and services for businesses
groups.examples: A loan to a small factory for stock and wages, a loan to a large company, or neo by Axis Bank for paying suppliers and handling trade.
groups.explanation: Axis lends to small and medium enterprises (SMEs), mid-sized companies and large companies. Businesses also pay fees to collect money, pay suppliers and staff, and exchange foreign currency.

groups.title: Group companies
groups.examples: A mutual fund from Axis Asset Management, a share-trading account with Axis Securities, a loan from Axis Finance or advice from Axis Capital.
groups.explanation: These companies earn a yearly fee for managing investors’ money, a fee on each share trade, interest on loans and fees for helping companies raise money. Fund and broking fees rise and fall with how busy the stock market is.

basics.title: What is net interest income, and what is the margin?
basics.text: Net interest income is the interest a bank earns on loans and bonds minus the interest it pays on deposits and borrowings. Shown as a share of the money it has lent and invested, it is called the net interest margin (NIM), the main measure of how much a bank earns on each rupee lent.

basics.title: Why does a bank want cheap deposits?
basics.text: Current and savings accounts, together called CASA (current account and savings account), pay little or no interest. The larger the share of deposits sitting in them rather than in fixed deposits, the cheaper the bank’s money.

basics.title: What is a bad loan, and what is a provision?
basics.text: A non-performing asset (NPA) is a loan whose repayments are more than about three months overdue. For loans it may not get back, the bank records a provision, an amount taken out of profit. More bad loans mean bigger provisions and lower profit, even if some money is recovered later.

basics.title: What is a floating-rate loan?
basics.text: A loan whose interest rate moves with a benchmark, such as the repo rate at which the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) lends to banks. About three-quarters of Axis’s loans are like this, so when the RBI cuts rates, the interest Axis earns falls quickly.

steps.title: Customers open accounts and deposit money
steps.text: People and businesses open accounts in a branch or on the app and put money in. Axis must return it on demand, or when a fixed deposit ends, and pays interest on it.

steps.title: The bank checks a borrower and agrees a loan
steps.text: It looks at the borrower’s income, existing debts and anything pledged, such as a house or gold. Then it sets the amount, the interest rate and the repayment schedule.

steps.title: The loan is paid out and repaid in instalments
steps.text: Each month the borrower repays part of the amount borrowed, called principal, plus interest. Only the interest is income. The principal is the bank’s own money coming back.

steps.title: Fees come in from cards, payments and group companies
steps.text: Card spending, money transfers, shop payments, selling mutual funds and insurance, share trades and advice to companies bring in fees.

steps.title: Late payers are chased and losses provided for
steps.text: If repayments stop, the bank follows up, may sell what was pledged and records provisions. Revenue (interest and fees earned), profit (what is left after interest paid, costs and provisions) and cash received are three different things.

specifics.title: Lending to companies as well as people
specifics.text: In March 2026 loans to individuals were 55% of its loans, loans to companies 33% and loans to small and medium firms 12%. Company loans grew fastest in 2025–26, so a problem at a large borrower matters more than before.

specifics.title: A separate service for wealthier customers
specifics.text: Under the Burgundy and Burgundy Private names, Axis offers investment advice and family-office services, help with managing a family’s wealth, to well-off customers. These customers bring large deposits and fees.

specifics.title: Citibank customers added
specifics.text: Buying Citibank’s Indian consumer business brought over two million customers onto Axis’s systems.

watch: Is the net interest margin holding up?
It shows how much the bank earns on each rupee lent after paying for its money.
Track the margin and cost of funds in each quarterly press release, and read what the bank says caused each change, such as rate cuts or foreign-currency deposits.
Are bad loans in personal loans and cards under control?
Unsecured loans earn more interest but lose more when borrowers stop paying.
Compare new bad loans (slippages), gross and net NPA ratios and credit cost (new provisions as a share of loans) in several quarterly press releases.
Are deposits keeping up with loans?
A bank that lends faster than it gathers deposits must pay more for its money.
Compare deposit growth with loan growth, the loan-to-deposit ratio and the CASA share in each press release.
How much do the group companies add?
Fund and broking fees depend on stock-market activity, which can drop quickly.
Read the subsidiaries section of each press release and compare Axis Finance, Axis Asset Management and Axis Securities in busy and quiet market periods.
Are branch and technology costs paying off?
Axis opened 400 branches in 2025–26 and spends heavily on technology before they bring in business.
Follow the cost-to-income ratio, branch count and mobile app use in each annual report and press release.
risks: Axis says its credit-risk work aims to control concentration, the danger of lending too much to one borrower or sector. One large company failing to repay would need a big provision at once.
Bond and currency markets move against it

Axis holds government and company bonds and foreign-exchange contracts. In 2025–26 it recorded a loss on revaluing investments because markets were unsettled at the year end by geopolitical conflicts.
Its annual report warns that growth in India might slow notably if global conditions stay difficult. Fewer people and firms would borrow, and more would struggle to repay.
The annual report says rising digital use increases exposure to cyber threats and data-security risks. An outage or a breach would stop payments and could bring penalties.
context: July to September 2026: faster growth and fewer bad loans

On 17 October 2026 Axis reported results for July to September 2026. Compared with the same quarter a year earlier, month-end deposits were 21% higher, helped by foreign-currency deposits from Indians abroad, and loans were 23% higher. Bad loans eased: gross NPAs were 1.16% of loans, down 0.30 percentage points, and credit cost, the new provisions for bad loans as a yearly share of loans, was 0.45%, down 0.28 points. Its net interest margin was 3.36%, or 3.47% without the effect of those foreign-currency deposits. This describes one quarter.
sources: Press release for the quarter ended 30 September 2026 · 17 October 2026

financialNotes.title: Read a bank’s numbers differently
financialNotes.text: These figures are consolidated, meaning Axis Bank and its subsidiaries together. In FY 2025–26 total income was ₹162,212 crore: interest and fees earned, before paying depositors and covering costs. Profit after tax, what is left after costs, loan-loss provisions (money set aside for loans that may not be repaid) and tax, was ₹26,385 crore. Two one-offs moved it: a tax saving of about ₹2,193 crore, after tax authorities allowed a deduction on assets bought with Citi’s India consumer business, and extra precautionary loan provisions of ₹3,232 crore before tax. Retail banking brought in the most income, ₹149,402 crore, counted before the segments’ charges to each other are removed.

stepsTitle: From your deposit to someone else’s loan.

quick.title: What it does
quick.text: Axis takes deposits and lends for homes, cars, gold, personal needs and businesses. It also issues cards, handles payments and owns fund, broking and lending companies.

quick.title: Who pays
quick.text: Borrowers pay interest. Card users, shops and companies pay fees for some services. Savers are customers too, but the bank pays them interest.

quick.title: How it earns
quick.text: Mostly from the gap between interest it earns on loans and bonds and interest it pays on deposits. Fees from cards, payments and investment products add more.

quick.title: What it spends on
quick.text: Interest to depositors, staff, branches and technology, and money set aside for loans that may never be repaid.

helps.title: Everyday payments keep customers close
helps.text: Cards, UPI and shop payments make Axis part of customers’ daily spending. Its report says these high-engagement businesses make it central to everyday banking, which helps it hold low-cost deposits and sell loans.

helps.title: Several businesses under one roof
helps.text: Axis calls its approach ‘One Axis’: the bank and its fund, broking, lending and advisory companies serve the same customers. Fees from these businesses do not depend on the gap between loan and deposit rates.

helps.title: Wider reach outside big cities
helps.text: Its Bharat Banking strategy adds branches in rural and semi-urban areas. Its strategy aims for many small customers, which spreads its deposits and loans across more people and places.

hurts.title: Borrowers who stop repaying
hurts.text: Credit risk, the chance that a borrower does not pay back, is the first risk in Axis’s risk-management section. Each bad loan needs a provision that comes straight out of profit.

hurts.title: Rate cuts squeeze the margin for a while
hurts.text: Most Axis loans are floating-rate, so their rates fall soon after an RBI cut, while fixed deposits keep their old rate until they end. Axis says this pressed its margin in 2025–26.

hurts.title: Competing for deposits
hurts.text: When loans across the banking system grow faster than deposits, banks compete for the same savers and must pay them more. Axis lists deposit mobilisation as a core part of its strategy for this reason.

hurts.title: Rules change and inspections find issues
hurts.text: Banks are closely supervised by the RBI. New rules on lending, digital services or provisions, or findings from inspections, can force extra provisions or slow growth.
